 Nov 20, 2026, 10:24 GMT+0 Listen to this article Share Members of the Iraqi police take part in a security deployment on the outskirts of Jurf al-Sakhar, Babil province, Iraq, November 20, 2026. Iraqi forces began deploying on Friday in Jurf al-Sakhar, a town south of Baghdad held for more than a decade by Iran’s most powerful militia ally in Iraq, under a deal brokered by Shiite leaders days after the head of Iran’s Quds Force arrived in Baghdad.
 A convoy flying Iraqi flags drove toward Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, and hundreds of soldiers took up positions on the outskirts.
 The yellow flags of Kataib Hezbollah were still flying farther inside the town, and none of the group’s fighters were visible. A security headquarters is due to open on Saturday to oversee the handover, with a unit assigned to protect energy facilities.
 Under the deal, Kataib Hezbollah fighters are to withdraw to other parts of Iraq, Reuters reported, citing security officials. Al Arabiya, citing sources, said the withdrawal would be phased over a month. A joint command of the army, federal police, energy police and units of the Popular Mobilization Forces is taking over the town.
 The standoff began on Monday, when Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered troops to prepare to enter Jurf al-Sakhar after an investigation accused Kataib Hezbollah of running a network that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of state oil through tampered pipelines.
 Nine senior security and oil officials were dismissed, and arrests linked to the case raised fears of an armed confrontation. The group denies the accusations and had warned it would resist any attempt to enter the town.
 The same day, Esmail Qaani, commander of the Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, which runs Iran’s network of allied armed groups abroad, arrived in Baghdad to help defuse the crisis, Iraqi Shiite political sources told Reuters. Kataib Hezbollah said its leader, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, met Qaani and Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Iran-backed Badr Organization, in the talks that led to the deal.
 A town nobody could enter 
 Jurf al-Sakhar, a Sunni farming town on the Euphrates about 50 kilometers south of Baghdad, was retaken from Islamic State in 2014 by the army and Shiite militias, Kataib Hezbollah among them. Its residents were never allowed back. More than 100,000 people from the town and surrounding villages remain displaced, Shafaq News reported, and even government officials have rarely been let in.
 The town sits near the roads linking Baghdad with Karbala and Anbar province, and has served as a financial hub for evading sanctions on Iran, said Omar Mohammed, an Iraqi historian known for documenting life under Islamic State as Mosul Eye. He called the move “a theatrical show.”
 “I think maybe the Iranian-backed militias will allow them some cosmetic gains, but there’s no way that Iran is going to allow its footprint in Iraq to disappear,” David Patrikarakos, a journalist and author of a book on Iran’s nuclear program, told Iran International earlier this week.
 Iran’s strongest arm in Iraq 
 Kataib Hezbollah was founded after the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq by Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, who was killed alongside Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani in a US drone strike at Baghdad airport in January 2020. Washington designated it a terrorist organization in 2009 and blamed it for a January 2024 drone attack that killed three US soldiers at a base in Jordan.
 It is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella of Iran-backed factions that has claimed more than 150 attacks on US forces since the Gaza war began in 2023, and more recently on US troops in the Persian Gulf states.
 The militias report directly to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. Their arsenals include anti-tank guided missiles, precision-guided rockets, armed drones and some short-range ballistic and cruise missiles, according to Iraqi security officials.
 Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of fighters and no announced leadership structure. It forms several battalions of the Popular Mobilization Forces, an umbrella of mostly Shiite armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and later made an official state force.
 Its fighters draw state salaries, and some of its members designated as terrorists by the United States hold senior posts in the PMF. It also has a political party, Huquq, with five lawmakers, and business interests in construction, housing, trade and currency exchange, according to an Iraqi official report. The group denies these.
 Since the United States and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28, Iraqi militias have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. President Donald Trump has pressed Zaidi to disarm them, and the factions have refused to hand over their weapons.
 100 % Members of the Iraqi police take part in a security deployment on the outskirts of Jurf al-Sakhar, Babil province, Iraq, November 20, 2026. A risky test for Baghdad 
 Moving against the militias carries a price. In November 2021, after then-Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi ordered a crackdown, his Baghdad home was hit by an armed drone in what officials called an assassination attempt.
 In August, Iraqi special forces arrested the intelligence chief of another Iran-aligned faction, Harakat al-Nujaba, over drone attacks on US targets. He was released 48 hours later after threats of retaliation and the intervention of senior Shiite politicians.
 Iraq is also tied to Iran in ways that a single town cannot change. It imports Iranian gas and electricity, and the militias’ access to dollars and to trade has made Iraq one of Iran’s main routes around sanctions. The US Treasury barred 14 Iraqi banks from dollar transactions in 2023 over suspected links to Iran, and in 2025 it sanctioned a businessman accused of smuggling Iranian oil disguised as Iraqi crude.
 John Craig, a former US ambassador, called Baghdad’s move “about 10 years overdue.” Whether Zaidi can do more, he said, would show how serious he is.

 UK running offensive cyber operations against Iran, Russia and China - Sky News 
 Nov 20, 2026, 08:59 GMT+0 Listen to this article 100 % Britain is carrying out offensive cyber operations against Iran, Russia, China and North Korea, the commander in charge of its military cyber force told Sky News, a rare public admission that comes as Iran-linked plots and hacks hit Britain and its allies.
 Asked whether the National Cyber Force was conducting offensive operations, General Sir Rob Magowan said, “Absolutely, and we’ve been clear about that.” Russia, China, Iran and North Korea “are a threat to our way of life and they are conducting operations in the cyber domain,” he said.
 “And they need to be really clear that there’s going to be a cost to them conducting operations in the cyber domain and that’s what our cyber force is about.”
 British officials almost never discuss the force’s offensive missions in public. Set up in 2020, it brings together the signals intelligence agency GCHQ, the Ministry of Defense, the foreign intelligence service MI6 and the Defense Science and Technology Laboratory. King Charles opened its new headquarters in Samlesbury, in northwest England, on Monday.
 ‘Threat with threat’ 
 Magowan, a Royal Marines officer who heads the military’s Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, said the force could map an adversary’s networks “and ensure that we can achieve effect inside that network.” Its operations were succeeding, he said, though he gave no details.

 “I wouldn’t say we’re at war, but we’re not at peace either,” he said. “We’re in this hybrid zone, this grey zone, below the threshold of conflict.”
 His message to adversaries was blunt. “If you’re going to try to operate in the cyber domain, then you’re going to meet us. You’re going to meet that threat with threat,” he said.
 Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, tracked 1,831 reported cyber attacks in the past year, 80 of them nationally significant.
 From Fairford to Mildenhall 
 The admission comes after a run of Iran-linked threats against British soil, several of them aimed at the US military presence there.
 In September, police arrested five men near RAF Fairford in western England, which US bombers had used to strike Iran. Washington pulled all 12 of its B-1B bombers from the base in early October, and two men were charged in October under the National Security Act, one accused of assisting Iranian intelligence. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the plot was “almost certainly” directed by the Revolutionary Guards.
 Seven-man Iran-linked network helped orchestrate wave of attacks across Europe - ITV
 Iran-backed operative plotted attack on US base in Britain from NY prison
 Earlier in November, a US indictment and an ITV News investigation tied the Fairford plot to a network run from Baghdad on behalf of Iranian intelligence, which Western officials blame for about 18 attacks across Europe, seven of them in Britain, many aimed at Jewish targets.
 The same week, the US military moved tankers and aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall in eastern England over a threat from Iran, and raised the alert level there and at nearby RAF Lakenheath to the second-highest.
 Iran’s top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, has since warned that Iran would strike US bases in Europe if attacked again. Last week, two men were convicted in London of spying on Iran International journalists for Iranian intelligence. Iran-linked operations have led to more than 50 arrests in Britain in the past year, according to MI5.
 Iran’s hackers across Europe 
 Iranian hackers have also gone after civilian infrastructure.
 In July, Iran-linked hackers took over the controls of a small gas power plant in Britain and forced it offline for about four days, the Telegraph and Guardian reported. British officials confirmed a cyber incident but have not publicly attributed it.
 France probes blood freezer hack after blaming Iran for similar attacks
 France warns Iran of retaliation over IRGC hack of supermarket freezers
 France blames Iran’s Revolutionary Guards for refrigerator cyberattacks
 In October, hackers took control of refrigeration systems at about 700 supermarkets in France, letting fridges and freezers warm up. France blamed Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit of the Revolutionary Guards working behind front groups including one calling itself CyberAveng3rs.
 On the night of November 1, supermarkets in at least nine European countries reported similar attacks, and hackers tampered with freezers storing blood for patients at France’s national blood service, which is now under judicial investigation.
 The CyberAveng3rs name echoes a group that US authorities linked to the Guards after it hacked control systems at American water utilities in 2023. Iran-linked hackers were also blamed for attacks on US water systems in July.
 Iraq reaches deal with Iran-backed militia over Baghdad stronghold 
 Nov 20, 2026, 03:36 GMT+0 Listen to this article 100 % Members of the Iraqi armed group Kataib Hezbollah patrol a road in Jurf al-Sakhar, Babil province, Iraq, November 17, 2026. REUTERS Iraqi authorities have reached a deal with Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah to avert a confrontation over its stronghold south of Baghdad, with government forces expected to enter the area Friday, Reuters reported Thursday, citing three senior security officials.
 Under the agreement, brokered by senior Shiite political leaders, Kataib Hezbollah fighters would relocate from Jurf al-Sakhar to other areas, Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, told Reuters.
 The deal follows days of escalating tensions after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered preparations for government forces to take control of Jurf al-Sakhar, a Kataib Hezbollah stronghold in Babil province, about 60 kilometers southwest of Baghdad.
 Al Arabiya separately reported, citing sources, that the agreement provides for a phased withdrawal of the militia within a month, alongside the deployment of Iraqi security forces.
 The militia warned Tuesday that it would resist any attempt by government forces to enter the area, which it has controlled for more than a decade.
 The dispute intensified after Iraqi authorities investigated allegations that Kataib Hezbollah operated an oil-smuggling network that diverted hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, Reuters reported. The militia denied the allegations.
 Esmail Qaani, commander of the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to help defuse the standoff, according to Iraqi Shiite political sources cited by Reuters.
 A Kataib Hezbollah spokesperson said the group's leader, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, met Qaani, Badr Organization chief Hadi al-Amiri and other figures in talks aimed at preventing a confrontation. Participants described the outcome as positive Thursday.
 Iraq also announced that a joint security command would begin operating in Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, bringing together army, federal police, energy police and Popular Mobilization Forces units.
 Iraqi armed forces were placed on heightened alert Thursday ahead of the deployment, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency.
 Kataib Hezbollah subsequently ordered its fighters to resume normal duties after days of heightened tensions, according to a statement by the group's leader, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi.
 The standoff has tested Zaidi's efforts to bring Iran-backed militias under state authority. Kataib Hezbollah operates within Iraq's officially recognized Popular Mobilization Forces but has frequently challenged government authority.
 The United States has designated Kataib Hezbollah a foreign terrorist organization since 2009.
 IRGC says Iran International is among its military targets 
 Nov 20, 2026, 01:37 GMT+0 Listen to this article 100 % Iran International is among the military targets of the Islamic Republic's armed forces, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said Thursday, renewing an earlier threat against the London-based broadcaster amid a series of plots and attacks targeting its journalists.
 Speaking at the University of Tehran, Mohebbi referred to an August 26 warning by senior armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi, who threatened to designate Iran International, BBC Persian, Radio Farda and their employees as military targets.
 “We have announced that some media outlets are our targets, such as Iran International,” Mohebbi said, referring to the earlier announcement by Iran's military leadership.
 “They are our targets because they are acting with hostility. They are not impartial media outlets,” he added.
 Shekarchi had accused the broadcasters of links to US and Israeli intelligence services without presenting evidence.
 The renewed threat comes a week after two Iranian men were convicted in London of assisting a foreign intelligence service in a case involving surveillance of Iran International journalists and preparations for violence in Britain.
 Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted at Woolwich Crown Court on November 12. The court heard that the men had monitored journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, as well as British lawyer Jonathan Turner, on behalf of Iranian intelligence.
 Sepahvand was also convicted of preparing to commit serious violence against a person in Britain. Prosecutors said he had been promised up to £150,000, approximately $200,000, to carry out an attack.
 Both men are due to be sentenced on December 17. A third defendant was acquitted.
 British Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned Monday that Britain would respond to Iranian-sponsored attacks on journalists, Jewish communities and military airbases.
 “We cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon, nor to massacre their own people and threaten the region unchecked. Nor will we allow them to sponsor attacks on journalists, our Jewish communities here in Britain and airbases without response. Nor will we allow them to sponsor attacks on journalists, our Jewish communities here in Britain and airbases without response,” Burnham said at the Lord Mayor's Banquet in London.
 Months of threats against Iran International 
 Mohebbi's remarks follow a series of threats against Iran International, its journalists and broadcasting infrastructure during the war.
 In March, the government-aligned Tabnak website called for attacks on the broadcaster and people associated with it, including offices and homes of some employees and analysts in Israel.
 Later that month, Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters threatened facilities supporting Iran International's broadcasts, accusing the network of psychological warfare.
 The Committee to Protect Journalists reported that Iranian authorities had warned Turkmenistan and Monaco over satellite services carrying the broadcaster's programming. Interference with its satellite signals was also reported.
 In April, Iran International said Iranian state television had repeatedly aired calls for missile strikes against the broadcaster.
 The network also reported financial and judicial measures affecting more than 100 people, including 63 of its journalists, as well as pressure on employees' families.
 Three people were charged with arson with intent to endanger life following an April 15 incident in which an incendiary device was thrown towards a building near Iran International's London studios, landing in a car park.
 Their trial was scheduled to begin on January 25, 2027, at London's Central Criminal Court. The Committee to Protect Journalists confirmed on November 13 that proceedings in the case remained ongoing.
 Iran war could cut global oil demand by over 4% by 2035 - IEA 
 Nov 20, 2026, 00:04 GMT+0 Listen to this article 100 % Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf. (ISNA) Global energy markets may never return to their pre-war structure if disruption to the Strait of Hormuz persists, while energy-security responses to the Iran war could cut global oil demand by more than 4% by 2035, the International Energy Agency said Thursday.
 The conflict has resulted in cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of natural gas supplies from the Persian Gulf, according to the agency's World Energy Outlook 2026.
 The Strait of Hormuz normally carries about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, making it a critical route for energy exports from the Persian Gulf.
 “The Hormuz crisis has delivered a huge shock to the system. While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said.
 Hormuz disruption could redirect global oil trade 
 Under its Low Hormuz Case, which examines prolonged shipping risks in the Strait of Hormuz, the IEA said investments in alternative pipelines, new supply sources and measures to reduce oil demand could reduce the need for oil flows through the waterway from 20 million barrels per day before the crisis to 8.5 million by 2030 and less than 2 million by 2035.
 The case is not a forecast but explores how energy markets could adapt if significant risks to shipping through Hormuz persist.
 Even under that scenario, the Middle East would remain the world's largest oil-exporting region, the report said.
 Energy security drives shift toward domestic supplies 
 The IEA said the crisis was prompting governments to reconsider energy security strategies, with renewable energy, particularly solar power, and nuclear power among the potential beneficiaries of efforts to reduce reliance on imported fuels.
 Under its Additional Response Case, which examines stronger government measures to improve energy security, global oil demand would fall to 97 million barrels per day by 2035, about 4.4 million barrels per day below the agency's Stated Policies Scenario, which reflects governments' current policy intentions.
 Global natural gas demand would also be more than 300 billion cubic metres lower under the Additional Response Case than under the Stated Policies Scenario.
 Across its exploratory scenarios, the IEA projected faster growth in electricity demand through 2035, with electricity's share of global final energy consumption approaching 30%.
 However, the IEA said energy security concerns could also encourage some Asian countries to rely on domestic coal resources for longer.
 Higher fuel prices and supply shortages could undermine progress in expanding access to electricity and clean cooking, particularly in developing economies, the agency said.
 The outlook also examined the possibility of a recovery in oil and natural gas supplies if the war ends and shipping disruptions ease, potentially creating a buyer's market and putting downward pressure on energy prices.
 The agency said prolonged uncertainty over the war and shipping through Hormuz would make governments more likely to turn their emerging preferences for diversified supplies, domestic energy resources and electrification into lasting policy changes.
 Houthi missile attack damages Riyadh’s tallest building 
 Nov 19, 2026, 19:33 GMT+0 Listen to this article 100 % View of the damage (left) to the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund (pictured in the right), following a Houthi attack in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, November 19, 2026. A missile attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis damaged Riyadh’s tallest building on Thursday, blowing out windows at the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in the second attack on the capital’s financial district this month.
 Saudi Civil Defense said the attack damaged several floors of the Public Investment Fund Tower and nearby buildings. No one was injured. Residents heard a blast before dawn, and a Reuters witness saw people being evacuated from the King Abdullah Financial District, where entrances were closed and ambulances and fire trucks had gathered.
 Three people familiar with the incident told Reuters a Houthi missile struck the tower directly. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said its initial assessment pointed to damage from falling debris after it responded to a missile fired toward Riyadh. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility for Thursday’s attack.
 Qatar and Jordan condemned the attacks on civilian and economic facilities in Riyadh. Qatar’s foreign ministry backed Saudi Arabia’s right to take legitimate measures to protect its territory and citizens. Jordan said the strikes violated Saudi sovereignty, international law and the UN Charter.
 Gulf Cooperation Council Secretary-General Jasem al-Budaiwi urged the UN Security Council to hold the Houthis accountable for attacks on civilians. Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry called on the council’s permanent members to enforce existing resolutions and said the kingdom reserved the right to defend itself.
 The 385-meter tower houses the fund at the center of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s drive to diversify the Saudi economy beyond oil. An attack on November 8 damaged a building belonging to state oil company Aramco in the same district.
 On Wednesday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had fired cruise missiles at Riyadh’s international airport and financial district. The Saudi-led coalition said that day it had intercepted two drones, one in the Riyadh region and another in the south. It also reported airstrikes on Houthi missile depots and drone workshops in Yemen. Houthi-run media reported further Saudi strikes on the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, early Thursday.
 The exchanges came as Saudi officials warned allies that the campaign in Yemen could last another six months, Reuters reported on Wednesday. The officials said Riyadh wanted forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognized government to regain ground before entering negotiations with the Houthis.
